extracted.intended_audience: OMB, agency regulatory analysts, policymakers, and stakeholders preparing or reviewing Regulatory Impact Analyses (RIAs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for preparing, reviewing, and updating Regulatory Impact Analyses (RIAs) and benefit-cost analyses used by U.S. federal agencies under OMB Circular A-4. Focuses on transparency, scope, baselines, discounting, distributional treatment, uncertainty, and learning/retrospective evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of methods and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: RIAs must be transparent about the key methods, data, analytical choices, inclusion and exclusion of effects, and any data limitations or other sources of uncertainty regarding who will experience regulatory impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should aim for transparency about methods, data and analytical choices (quoting OMB 2023). Explain the basis for decisions on inclusion/exclusion of effects and be clear about limitations. Anti-pattern: burying key assumptions or omitting domestic impacts when they can be separated. Scoring note: analyses that clearly document methods, data sources, and rationale score highest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of RIA (inform not determine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory impact analysis informs policy decisions by presenting welfare differences and efficiency implications, but does not determine policy decisions; other factors (legal constraints, political viability, practicality, distributional concerns) also matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present neutral, objective estimates of consequences (good and bad) for alternatives. Anti-pattern: conflating analytic conclusions with policy prescriptions or embedding normative choices without disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and justify the need for regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must identify the core problem the regulation intends to address (including market or public institution failures) and assess the significance of that problem; analysis should not presuppose the need for regulation or its effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the compelling public need qualitatively and when possible quantitatively; demonstrate why federal regulation is necessary rather than relying on assumptions. Anti-pattern: assuming regulatory need or effectiveness up front; failing to demonstrate a material market failure or significant public need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain economic regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a presumption against certain types of economic regulation—e.g., price controls in well-functioning competitive markets, production/sales quotas, mandatory uniform quality standards when voluntary alternatives suffice, and controls on entry—unless a particularly demanding burden of proof is met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should require strong evidence of net benefits before imposing such regulations. Anti-pattern: treating such interventions as routine or failing to acknowledge potential for regulatory harm and rent-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for using behavioral justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Before overriding individuals' revealed preferences based on behavioral claims, agencies should provide situation-specific evidence that individuals behave irrationally (and do not learn) in the specific situation covered by the proposed regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of internality arguments; acknowledge that government actors may share biases. Permissible use: carefully formed nudges and informational approaches when evidence supports their effectiveness. Anti-pattern: using generic behavioral claims without situational evidence to justify intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for federalism and state/local solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider whether state, local, territorial, or Tribal authorities can address problems effectively before asserting federal preemption; deferring to subnational solutions supports learning and natural experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage learning value of deferring to states when interstate commerce not implicated; avoid open-ended language that invites overriding states absent clear demonstration. Anti-pattern: defaulting to federal action without evaluating state capacity or alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope of analysis (domestic primary focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary RIA analysis should generally focus on effects experienced by U.S. citizens and residents; if the primary analysis is global, agencies should also produce a separate supplementary analysis of effects on U.S. citizens/residents unless separation is impractical or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always present domestic estimates so policymakers/public can see distributional effects in the U.S. Anti-pattern: presenting only global impacts or hiding domestic harms in a global-centric analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of benefit-cost analysis (include significant consequences but draw objective boundaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: BCA should include all significant direct and indirect, intended and unintended consequences of a policy, but agencies must draw boundaries objectively and transparently and distinguish 'additional' (ancillary) benefits/costs from primary impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should avoid selectively including favorable ancillary benefits while omitting additional costs; clearly label impacts related to the main purpose versus unrelated benefits/costs. Legal note: counting effects outside enabling statute can invite judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of 'additional' (ancillary) benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may consider benefits/costs unrelated to the regulation's main purpose, but must distinguish them from direct effects and ensure objective, balanced boundary-setting; avoid blurring statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly separate additional/ancillary items from primary impacts; explain why including them is analytically and legally appropriate. Anti-pattern: using 'additional' benefits to make preferred options appear more cost-effective while ignoring additional costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline selection (pre‑statutory baseline preferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should use a pre-statutory baseline by default; using a post-statutory baseline that treats statutory requirements as already implemented should be rare and justified with clear examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-statutory baseline provides transparency for Congress, courts, and the public; agencies may present post-statutory comparisons as supplemental but should not omit pre-statutory estimates. Anti-pattern: excluding statutory elements from the baseline without clear justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for compliance and take-up (compliance assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must clearly present key assumptions about compliance and take-up; assuming partial compliance without discussion may obscure true expected costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence suggests imperfect compliance, explain implications and consider whether alternative approaches are needed. Anti-pattern: presenting only partial compliance costs to understate full burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional impacts—disaggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: RIAs should disaggregate effects to show how benefits and costs are distributed across income groups, disadvantaged, vulnerable, or marginalized communities, and other affected populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, transparent presentation of who gains and who bears costs; disaggregation is especially important for rules affecting basic goods/services. Anti-pattern: only reporting aggregate net benefits without distributional detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional weights (do not embed in BCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should present traditionally-weighted benefits and costs and transparent distributional information, but should not embed distributional weights in the primary BCA because weights introduce non‑transparent normative judgments and can swamp efficiency analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present unweighted BCA plus separate distributional analyses; let policymakers make normative tradeoffs. Anti-pattern: applying interpersonal utility weights in a way that obscures normative choices or misleads about analytic precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of timing and undiscounted streams
rubrics_metrics.description: As a first step, agencies should present undiscounted annual time streams of benefits, costs, and transfers, clearly identifying when impacts are expected to occur (start year and timing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting only snapshots at a future date; show full time profiles so readers can see when costs and benefits accrue. Anti-pattern: reporting only a single-year snapshot that masks timing of capital costs and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social discount rate—present range and avoid single normative rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Given uncertainty and sensitivity to assumptions, the Circular should not impose a single default social discount rate; agencies should present estimates across a range of reasonable discount rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain methodology for chosen rates, report results for multiple rates (e.g., including but not limited to 1.7%), and discuss implications. Anti-pattern: defaulting to one rate without sensitivity analysis; treating default as normative policy choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of private discount rates where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When modeling private behavior (e.g., consumer savings from appliances), agencies should use appropriate private discount rates faced by affected populations, ideally reflecting the distribution of rates across those populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is particularly important for understanding distributional impacts; do not characterize private rates as 'irrational' without evidence. Anti-pattern: applying a single public discount rate to private decisions that face different borrowing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of uncertainty—use expected values (assume risk neutrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: For regulatory policy affecting large populations, the expected value should serve as the central estimate of benefits and costs, accompanied by ranges that reflect uncertainty; assume risk neutrality unless compelling reasons exist otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected values reflect average payoffs over many trials and are appropriate for population-level policy. Anti-pattern: substituting risk-averse or behavioral probability distortions as central estimates without solid theoretical/empirical basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk aversion and behavioral adjustments to uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The draft should not depart from presenting expected values in favor of risk-averse formulations absent a clear, modelable theory of systematic errors in probability perception; behavioral risk adjustments are difficult to model robustly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If behavioral models are used, explain assumptions and limitations; avoid inconsistent treatment of behavioral insights (using them to justify interventions in some places but not others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of information (VoI) and designing regulations for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use VoI analysis to identify which uncertainties most affect conclusions and consider gathering additional information before rulemaking or designing regulations to enable learning (natural experiments, phased rollouts, real options).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When uncertainty materially affects net-benefit conclusions, consider delaying or collecting more info, or design rules to generate evaluable evidence. Agencies should evaluate whether research costs outweigh value of information. Anti-pattern: proceeding with irreversible, high-cost actions without considering VoI or learning designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective review and ex-post evaluation planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should design new regulations with ex-post evaluation and retrospective review in mind and plan periodic re-evaluation to identify outmoded, ineffective, or excessively burdensome rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate mechanisms for later assessment, data collection, and sunset or revision triggers. Tie to E.O. 13563 / E.O. 14094 and ACUS recommendations. Anti-pattern: failing to plan for or implement ex-post evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility and adaptation of risk assessment inputs for BCA
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide guidance for adapting risk assessment outputs to be compatible with BCA inputs, recognizing that risk assessment and BCA may use different metrics or assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit how to reconcile or translate risk assessment outputs into monetized or otherwise comparable BCA inputs; avoid silently importing inconsistent assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present benefits, costs, and transfers clearly; use opportunity cost concept
rubrics_metrics.description: RIAs should present benefits, costs, and transfers clearly and treat any use of resources as representing an opportunity cost equal to its next-best use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating transfers with net social costs; be explicit about when numbers represent transfers versus resource costs. Anti-pattern: treating transfers as societal resource costs without clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless complexity; encourage simpler timely analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize agency resource and expertise constraints; encourage simpler analyses earlier in the rulemaking process that can engage public input and improve evidence supporting outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simpler, timely BCAs where appropriate (back-of-envelope or preliminary analyses) to inform early decisions and public engagement. Anti-pattern: overcomplicating analyses such that they are unusable or obscure key issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directives in final Circular (recommended checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Circular should focus on economic efficiency and best estimates, avoid embedding normative factors in BCA, require a range of discount rates, present transparent distributional effects (not weights), assume risk neutrality (present expected values), present domestic alongside global estimates, and restore presumption against economic regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a synthesis of concrete recommendations (numbered items 1–6 in the comment) that agencies and OMB should adopt to retain objectivity and durability of A-4. Use as a high-level checklist when revising/assessing the Circular.
